h1: Brewing a stout that still sells in a hot Indian summer
title: A Stout That Sells in Indian Heat | Craft Beer School
desc: How brewpubs can design, serve and price a stout that keeps selling from April to June: lighter grists, nitro, serving temperature and menu placement.
teaser: Stout sales fall off a cliff in April. They do not have to, if the beer is built for the weather.
standfirst: Most brewpubs in India treat stout as a winter beer and watch it gather dust in summer. A stout designed for heat, with a drier body, lower strength and the right serve, can hold a tap through the hot months.
sections:
Customers associate dark beer with heavy beer. On a 40 °C afternoon in Delhi or Hyderabad they reach for lager, wheat beer or something fruity. The problem is often real: many brewpub stouts are 6 to 7% ABV, full bodied and sweet, which is a winter beer by any measure.

The colour itself is not the problem. A dry Irish-style stout at around 4 to 4.5% ABV is lighter in body than many pale ales. The task is to brew and present a stout that tastes as refreshing as it actually is.

Start from a dry stout rather than a sweet or imperial one. A practical target for a 1,000 litre batch: original gravity 1.040 to 1.042, final gravity 1.008 to 1.010, about 4.2% ABV and 30 to 40 IBU.

  • About 70% pale ale malt as the base.
  • About 10% roasted barley for the dry coffee bite.
  • About 10% flaked barley or oats for head retention. Keep oats modest, as heavy oats push the beer towards creamy and filling.
  • About 5% chocolate malt and 5% light caramel malt for roundness.

Mash at 65 to 66 °C so the beer ferments out. Keep caramel malt low. Sweetness is what makes a stout feel heavy in heat. Watch mash pH: roasted malts pull it down. With soft or RO water a stout can drop below 5.2 and turn sharp and acrid. A little calcium carbonate or sodium bicarbonate in the mash brings it back to 5.3 to 5.4.

Many brewpubs serve stout at the same temperature as their ales, or warmer, on the theory that dark beer needs warmth to show flavour. In summer, serve your session stout at about 5 to 6 °C. It will taste crisper and the roast will read as refreshing bitterness rather than heaviness.

Nitrogen dispense helps too. A nitro stout poured through a stout faucet with a restrictor plate gives a dense, creamy head and soft carbonation. Customers see the cascade and order another for the show. Nitro needs a beer blend gas line, the right faucet and lower CO2 in the beer, around 1.2 to 1.4 volumes. If you cannot run nitro, carbonate a little higher than usual, around 2.4 volumes, for lift.
Summer variants that keep the stout tap busy

A standard stout recipe can carry seasonal twists without a redesign:

  • Coffee stout using locally roasted Indian coffee, cold-steeped and added in the bright tank. Cold coffee is already a summer drink in Indian cities.
  • Coconut or cacao nib stout, light on sweetness.
  • A lighter milk stout at 4.5% with lactose kept below 5% of the grist. See our milk and oatmeal stout guide for the balance.

Each gives your staff something new to talk about without changing the base brew.

Menu placement matters as much as the recipe. Put the summer stout next to the lager on the tap card with a short line such as 'dry, roasty, 4.2%' so customers see it is not a heavy beer. Offer tasters. A 60 ml pour converts more stout sceptics than any description.

Food helps. A dry stout is excellent with grilled meat, kebabs and chocolate desserts, all common on brewpub menus. Train servers to suggest it with the mixed grill rather than waiting for someone to ask.

Price it the same as your other session beers. A stout priced as a premium beer looks like a winter indulgence.

Watch the glass too. A heavy dimpled mug signals a winter pint. A tall, slim nonic or a pilsner-style glass makes the same beer look like a summer drink.

A session stout fits into a wider seasonal plan. Brew the full-bodied stouts and porters for the winter months. Switch the dark tap to the dry session stout in March and keep it there through the monsoon. Our guide to planning a brewpub year around Indian seasons walks through the full calendar.

Track the dark tap's weekly sales across the year. If the session stout still lags far behind in May, adjust the serve and the menu before you blame the style.
faqs: What ABV should a summer stout be?
Around 4 to 4.5% ABV works well. That keeps it light enough for hot weather while still carrying roast flavour.
Does nitro really help stout sales?
It often does in a taproom, because the cascade and creamy head draw attention and the soft carbonation makes the beer feel smooth. It needs the right gas, faucet and carbonation level to work.
Why does my stout taste acrid with RO water?
Roasted malts lower mash pH. With soft water the pH can fall too far, which makes roast taste harsh. Add a little alkalinity to bring the mash back to about 5.3 to 5.4.
Can I use Indian coffee in a stout?
Yes. Cold-steeped coffee added after fermentation gives clean coffee aroma. Add it to taste in small trials and use it fresh.
